items.prompt: Explain why wage records can understate women’s contribution to family welfare.
items.canonical_answer: They can omit unpaid care, food and household production that support well-being. No recorded wage therefore does not establish no work or contribution.
marking_guidance: Reason: connect the measurement boundary to omitted useful activity.

items.canonical_answer: Women may perform paid work such as selling produce. Unpaid farming or household production also supplies goods and services even when no wage is recorded.

items.prompt: Explain how culture and position can influence women’s opportunities.
items.canonical_answer: Cultural values and practices influence expectations about work, property and participation. They can support cooperation or restrict opportunities depending on their form and use; culture is diverse and changing, not a fixed explanation of all women’s experiences.
marking_guidance: Reason: develop a link from an expectation or practice to access or voice, without treating all women’s experiences as identical.
Original indicative practice guidance; not an official mark scheme.

items.prompt: Explain the participation effect in a fictional village where meetings occur during women’s allocated water-collection time and decisions proceed without their input.
items.canonical_answer: The timetable makes attendance conflict with an assigned task, so those affected lose an opportunity to influence decisions. Changing time or sharing the collection task could reduce that particular barrier.
marking_guidance: Mechanism: time conflict linked to missing input.
Consequence: restricted influence; no assumption of lack of interest.

items.prompt: Explain how values can influence women’s opportunities.
items.canonical_answer: Values concern what people regard as desirable or acceptable. A value placed on mutual support may encourage shared work, while an expectation that leadership belongs to one gender can restrict voice. Explain the mechanism rather than stereotyping a community.
marking_guidance: Reason: develop a link from an expectation or practice to access or voice, without treating all women’s experiences as identical.
Original indicative practice guidance; not an official mark scheme.

items.prompt: Explain how customs can influence women’s opportunities.
items.canonical_answer: Customs and practices shape how social decisions are carried out. A meeting timetable or speaking arrangement can affect who participates. Consultation can reveal whether a practice supports or restricts access and what affected people want changed.
marking_guidance: Reason: develop a link from an expectation or practice to access or voice, without treating all women’s experiences as identical.

items.prompt: Explain how taboos and myths can influence women’s opportunities.
items.canonical_answer: A taboo restricts an activity or discussion; a myth may be used to explain or justify a belief. If a belief excludes women from a productive role regardless of skill, it narrows opportunity. Describing that effect does not endorse the belief or claim it is shared by all members.
marking_guidance: Reason: develop a link from an expectation or practice to access or voice, without treating all women’s experiences as identical.

items.prompt: Explain whether a fictional historical change establishes an overall improvement for women: wage work becomes available, but women lose food-growing access and retain the same unpaid workload. Judge livelihood choice and welfare.
items.canonical_answer: The wage opportunity may provide income, but reduced food access and unchanged unpaid burdens can offset it. An overall verdict needs earnings, food costs and workload evidence; wage availability alone does not establish improved choice or welfare.
marking_guidance: Judgement: weigh gains and losses against livelihood choice and welfare.
Reason: use all supplied changes and identify what evidence is missing.
Original indicative practice guidance; not an official mark scheme.

items.prompt: Describe this fictional historical comparison: before a change, women hold 60% of household food plots and 10% of paid jobs; afterwards, 30% of plots and 25% of paid jobs.
items.canonical_answer: Paid-job participation rises 15 percentage points while plot control falls 30 points. The two access measures move in opposing directions, so more paid work does not establish wider access to all productive resources.
marking_guidance: Evidence: accurate paired changes.
Relationship: contrast paid opportunity and plot control.
Original indicative practice guidance; not an official mark scheme.

items.prompt: Explain the opportunity or workload mechanism in this fictional historical case: comparable-skilled women are excluded from training while new jobs require its certificate.
items.canonical_answer: Exclusion prevents access to the recognised skill route and narrows eligibility for the new work.
marking_guidance: Mechanism, up to 2 marks: trace exclusion from training to inability to obtain the required certificate. Credit the stated factor and a valid causal link, not a disconnected list.
Consequence, 1 mark: link the certification barrier to narrower eligibility for the stated jobs.

items.prompt: Explain the opportunity or workload mechanism in this fictional historical case: commercial crops expand onto household food plots while women cannot decide how sales income is spent.

Consequence, 1 mark: link lack of control over crop income to restricted household or individual choices.

items.prompt: State (a) two useful measures of women’s contribution beyond wages [2]. Explain (b) why a fictional change bringing paid jobs but removing food-growing access cannot be judged from job numbers alone [4].
items.canonical_answer: (a) Food production and time spent providing care. (b) New paid work can increase money income, but counting jobs does not show the amount or reliability of those earnings. Losing growing land removes a source of household food and may reduce women’s control over productive resources. Purchasing replacement food can absorb some of the new income, while paid work may add to an unchanged care workload. Compare net resources, food access, time and decision-making control before judging whether overall welfare and choice improved.
marking_guidance: Point: two relevant non-wage measures [2].
Development: connect the opposing supplied changes to a bounded welfare judgement [4].
Original indicative practice guidance; not an official mark scheme.

items.prompt: Describe (a) this fictional comparison: A offers training at 40% participation and meetings at 20%; B offers 70% and 60% [3]. Suggest (b) a priority for A if both timetable clashes and lack of care cover are reported and the aim is fair access [3].
items.canonical_answer: (a) B combines higher training and meeting participation, by 30 and 40 percentage points. (b) Arrange workable times and care support with affected participants, then monitor access; those changes address stated barriers rather than interpreting low participation as unwillingness.
marking_guidance: Evidence: paired participation comparisons [3].
Meaning: action matched to both barriers and the fair-access aim [3].
Original indicative practice guidance; not an official mark scheme.
